Currently, there is insufficient information to determine minimum or maximum concentrations of minerals, as adequate intake depends on various factors. Therefore, no guideline values are proposed. 2. Heptachlor (CAS No. 76-44-8) is a broad-spectrum insecticide whose use has been banned or restricted in many countries. Its primary current application is for termite control through subsurface soil injection. Heptachlor is persistent in soil, where it is mainly converted to its epoxide form, heptachlor epoxide (CAS No. 1024-57-3), which is highly resistant to further degradation. Both heptachlor and heptachlor epoxide bind strongly to soil particles and migrate very slowly. They have been detected in drinking water at nanogram-per-liter levels. Dietary intake is considered the primary source of exposure, although this has significantly decreased due to reduced usage. 3. Prolonged exposure to heptachlor has been associated with liver damage and central nervous system toxicity. In 1991, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified heptachlor as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) based on sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in animals but inadequate evidence in humans. Heptachlor and its epoxide occur in drinking water at concentrations well below levels of health concern, making it unnecessary to establish a formal guideline value. 4. Hexachlorobenzene (HCB, CAS No. 118-74-1) was historically used as a seed dressing to prevent fungal growth in crops but is now primarily a by-product of chemical processes or an impurity in some pesticides. HCB is environmentally persistent, mobile, and bioaccumulative in organisms due to its physicochemical properties and slow elimination. It is commonly detected at low levels in food and ambient air. IARC has classified HCB as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) based on evidence of tumor induction in three animal species at various sites. A health-based value of 1 µg/L can be derived for HCB in drinking water, but concentrations in food and water are generally low, making a formal guideline value unnecessary. 5. Hexachlorobutadiene (HCBD) is used as a solvent in chlorine gas production, a pesticide, and an intermediate in rubber compound manufacturing. It is also found in air, food, and effluents from chemical plants. HCBD is metabolized via conjugation with glutathione, forming a nephrotoxic derivative. Kidney tumors have been observed in long-term oral studies in rats, but HCBD has not been shown to be carcinogenic via other exposure routes. IARC has classified HCBD as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans). Positive and negative results have been reported in bacterial assays for point mutations, with some metabolites showing positive results. 6. Hydrogen sulfide is formed when sulfides are hydrolyzed in water but is usually present at low levels in drinking water due to oxidation in well-aerated or chlorinated water. Acute toxicity from inhalation is high, with eye irritation occurring at 15–30 mg/m³. Oral toxicity data are lacking, but harmful doses from drinking water are unlikely. Consequently, no guideline value is proposed. Hydrogen sulfide can be detected in drinking water by taste or odor. 7. Tin is primarily used in coatings for the food industry, with canned food being the main source of human exposure. Drinking water is not a significant source, with levels above 1–2 µg/L being rare. Tin and inorganic tin compounds are poorly absorbed, do not accumulate in tissues, and are rapidly excreted. No increased tumor incidence has been observed in long-term carcinogenicity studies in animals. Acute gastric irritation is the main adverse effect of excessive tin levels in canned foods. Chronic exposure to tin has not been associated with adverse effects in humans. The presence of tin in drinking water does not pose a health hazard, and no guideline value is deemed necessary. 8. Iodine occurs naturally in water as iodide and is occasionally used for water disinfection in emergency situations. The diet is the primary source of iodine exposure, with drinking water contributing around 5%. Iodine is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis, with recommended daily intakes established by WHO/FAO. Excess iodine exposure can lead to thyroid dysfunction, including hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, and changes in thyroid malignancy incidence. However, data are insufficient to establish a dose-response relationship or a guideline value for iodine in drinking water. Iodine is not recommended for long-term disinfection, and lifetime exposure from water disinfection is unlikely. 9. Iron is one of the most abundant metals in the Earth's crust and is essential for human nutrition. Drinking water may contain iron due to the use of iron coagulants or corrosion of pipes. Iron levels in drinking water are not of health concern, but they may affect the taste and appearance of water. No guideline value is proposed for iron in drinking water. 10. Isoproturon (CAS No. 34123-59-6) is a selective herbicide used to control weeds in cereals. It is photodegradable, hydrolyzable, and biodegradable, with persistence ranging from days to weeks. Isoproturon has low acute toxicity and low to moderate toxicity following shortand long-term exposures. It does not exhibit significant genotoxic activity but causes enzyme induction and liver enlargement. Tumor promotion has been observed in rats at doses causing liver toxicity, suggesting it acts as a tumor promoter rather than a complete carcinogen.
